Tum, quod cotīdiē fit nec umquam sine certāmine, faciēs lavanda erat, dentēs pūrgandī. — Then came what happens every day and never without a fight: washing the face and brushing the teeth. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

id perfēcit quod puer coeperat, fricāns ubi ille lambuerat. «Ōs aperī. Lātius. Jam ēlue. Exspue. Satis est.» — he finished what the boy had begun, brushing where he had only licked. “Open your mouth. Wider. Now rinse. Spit. That’s enough.” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Ipse illinere volō! — I want to spread it myself! (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).

english: Curtain / rod / pole / track
keywords: Curtain / curtain rod / curtain pole / curtain track aulaeum virga aulaeī pertica aulaeī canālis aulaeī annulus fulcrum curtain rod pole rail track rings brackets Ancient words Modern formation open the curtains draw the curtains

items.html: aulaeum, aulaeī n. — curtain, hanging or drapery [Ancient Latin].
virga aulaeī — curtain rod; our preferred transparent formation for a slender cylindrical rod, such as the metal rod used with curtain rings.
pertica aulaeī — curtain pole; useful especially when the support is longer, thicker or more pole-like.
annulus aulaeī — curtain ring; plural annulī aulaeī.
fulcrum virgae — bracket/support for the rod; plural fulcra virgae.
virga extensilis aulaeī — extendable/telescoping curtain rod.
canālis aulaeī — curtain track/rail; a transparent modern formation based on ancient canālis “channel, groove.” Use this for a track system rather than a free-standing cylindrical rod.
Aulaeum ex virgā pendet. — The curtain hangs from the rod. Annulōs in virgam indūc. — Put the rings onto the rod.

Evidence note: the individual nouns are ancient. The compounds virga aulaeī, pertica aulaeī and canālis aulaeī are transparent modern formations; no strong lexicographic evidence was found that any one of them is an established traditional term. For the photographed slender metal rod, virga aulaeī is preferred.
aulaea, aulaeōrum n. pl. — curtains (Traupman 123); aulaea dīdūcere / obdūcere — open / draw the curtains.
Sed aulaeīs dīductīs nec arborēs nec montem nec lūmina vīdit — But when he opened the curtains he saw neither the trees nor the mountain nor the lights (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Pater igitur, aulaeīs obductīs lūmineque exstīnctō, puerum amplexus, Arīonem nārrāvit — So Dad drew the curtains, turned off the light, put his arm round the boy and told the story of Arion (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

keywords: electricity electric light lamp reading lamp socket outlet power point plug in charge phone alarm alarm clock radiator heating hair dryer vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: lūmen ēlectricum — electric light (Traupman 124); lūmen accendere / exstinguere — switch the light on / off, as in the open / close / switch-on entry.
lampas lēctōria — reading lamp (Traupman 124): classical lampas, lampadis f. “lamp, torch” with a modern adjective.

Tēlephōnum, in quō tesserae servābantur, pater capsulae contāctūs ēlectricī adnexuit — Dad plugged the phone, which held the tickets, into the socket (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Nōndum lūcēbat, cum suscitābulum sonuit. — It was not yet light when the alarm went off. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
computātrulum in mēnsā scrīptōriā aperuit, lampadem lēctōriam accendit — he opened the laptop on the desk and switched on the reading lamp (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
ubi inter librōrum pluteōs torī magnī tōmentō fartī stant calōrisque radiātrum tepet — where big stuffed sofas stand among the bookshelves and the radiator is warm (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
Ēgressum pater linteō tersit capillīsque īnstrūmentum siccātōrium admōvit. — When he got out, Dad dried him with a towel and held the hair dryer to his hair. (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).

english: Bathroom: washbasin / basin / mirror / shower / step stool
latin: lābellum, lābellī n. · speculum, speculī n.
keywords: bathroom washbasin wash basin sink mirror shower take a shower step stool footstool vocabulary 29 October fabulae Theodōrus et pater

items.html: lābellum, lābellī n. — washbasin, sink (Traupman 125). Classically a small basin or tub (Cato, Agr. 10.2; Columella). Long ā with de Vaan, from lavābrum; Lewis & Short prints a short a.
lābrum, lābrī n. — basin, tub (Cic. Fam. 14.20 labrum sī in balineō nōn est); the bath-time entry keeps it apart from labrum, lip.
speculum, speculī n. — mirror (Plaut.; Varro, LL 5.129); in speculō spectāre — look in the mirror.
balneum pluvium; balneolum pluvium — shower (Traupman 124: cubiculum balneō pluviō īnstrūctum); balneolō pluviō ūtor — I take a shower (Traupman 124).
scabellum, scabellī n. — step stool, footstool (Varro, LL 5.168; Cato, Agr. 10.4); Varro derives it from scandere: wrongly, since it is the diminutive of scamnum.

Ad lābrum Theodōrus, in scabellō stāns, pēniculum dentārium, dentifriciō illitum, ipse tenuit et ipse mōvit — At the basin, standing on the step stool, Theo held the toothbrush with the toothpaste on it and moved it himself (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

pater autem, post eum stāns et in speculō spectāns, id perfēcit quod puer coeperat — Dad, standing behind him and watching in the mirror, finished what the boy had begun (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Theodōrus, priusquam exīret, ad lābellum minimum manūs lāvit. — Before he came out, Theo washed his hands at the tiny basin. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
In cubiculō, quod balneō pluviō īnstrūctum erat, duo lectī erant et fenestra. — In the room, which had a shower, there were two beds and a window. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

In cubiculō suō pater puerum, balneolō pluviō breviter lautum et linteō siccātum, synthesī dormītōriā vestīvit — In their room Dad gave the boy a quick shower, dried him with a towel and put his pyjamas on (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
